title: Late Decelerations -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Late decelerations are one of the precarious decelerations among the three types of fetal heart rate decelerations during labor. They are caused by decreased blood flow to the placenta and can signify an impending fetal acidemia. Late decelerations are defined as a visually apparent, gradual decrease in the fetal heart rate typically following the uterine contraction. A late deceleration typically follows a uterine contraction, meaning the onset, nadir, and return of the deceleration will follow the onset, peak, and return of a uterine contraction. This activity reviews the clinical significance of late decelerations and highlights the role of the interprofessional team in its management.

title: Late Decelerations -- Introduction
content: Late decelerations are among the most concerning of the 3 types of fetal heart rate decelerations during labor. They are caused by decreased blood flow to the placenta and can signify an impending fetal acidemia.

title: Late Decelerations -- Introduction -- Definition
content: Late deceleration is defined as a visually apparent, gradual decrease in the fetal heart rate that typically follows a uterine contraction. The gradual decline is defined as a period from onset to nadir that takes 30 seconds or more. A late deceleration typically follows a uterine contraction, meaning the onset, nadir, and return of the deceleration follow the onset, peak, and return of a uterine contraction. [1] Typically, late decelerations are shallow, with a slow onset and a gradual return to the normal baseline. The usual cause of the late deceleration is uteroplacental insufficiency.

title: Late Decelerations -- Etiology
content: The primary etiology of a late declaration is uteroplacental insufficiency, which results in decreased blood flow to the placenta and reduced blood and oxygen supply to the fetus. Some of the maternal and fetal conditions that can cause late decelerations are maternal dehydration, anemia, hypoxia, hypotension from epidural analgesia, uterine tachysystole, and placental abruption. [2] Any condition that predisposes to decreased uteroplacental blood flow can cause late decelerations. [3] [4]

title: Late Decelerations -- Epidemiology
content: Late decelerations are relatively common and correlate with uteroplacental insufficiency.

title: Late Decelerations -- Pathophysiology
content: The central pathophysiology of late deceleration involves uterine contractions constricting the uterine blood vessels, decreasing blood flow through the intervillous space of the placenta, reducing oxygen diffusion into fetal capillaries, and decreasing fetal PO 2 . When fetal PO 2 decreases, chemoreceptors trigger an autonomic response, leading to intense vasoconstriction and increased blood pressure. The elevated blood pressure is detected by baroreceptors, which ultimately stimulate the parasympathetic system to decrease the fetal heart rate, resulting in a late deceleration. [2] [4] The whole process reverses after the contraction is completed, with a relaxation of the uterine muscles allowing for increased blood flow to the placenta and resulting in the fetal heart rate returning to normal.

title: Late Decelerations -- Evaluation
content: Late decelerations are the most precarious decelerations among all types. Persistent and recurrent late decelerations need immediate, meticulous assessment to evaluate the cause and to rule out fetal acidemia. The 3-tier fetal heart rate tracing system is a valuable means for classifying the severity of fetal oxygenation status. [5] [6] It subdivides as follows: Category I is defined as having a baseline rate of 110 to 160 beats per minute, moderate baseline fetal heart rate (FHR) variability (amplitude 6 to 25 bpm), accelerations and early decelerations may be either present or absent, and no late or variable decelerations. Category III is defined as a fetal heart rate pattern with absent variability, recurrent variable, and late decelerations, bradycardia, or sinusoidal pattern. Category II is  any other FHR pattern that does not qualify for Category I or III.

title: Late Decelerations -- Evaluation
content: Foremost, the entire fetal heart rate tracing requires evaluation, including assessing uterine activity for tachysystole, the presence or absence of variability, and accelerations. [7] The fetal heart rate tracing is categorized as I, II, or III according to the criteria mentioned above. The presence of moderate variability and accelerations rules out acute fetal acidemia. [7] In the absence of variability and accelerations with persistent late decelerations, immediate attention is necessary as there may be ongoing fetal hypoxia resulting in metabolic acidosis. [4] [8] [9] Attention is also necessary for the full assessment of maternal status; this includes continuous monitoring of maternal vital signs, prevention of dehydration and maintenance of adequate intravascular volume, evaluation for ongoing bleeding, awareness of recent medication administration, and assessment of effects from epidural anesthesia. Any maternal hypotension should be addressed immediately.

title: Late Decelerations -- Treatment / Management
content: The principal goal of management of late decelerations is to: Replenish uteroplacental blood flow by correcting the underlying cause Increase fetal PO 2 Prevention or correction of fetal acidemia

title: Late Decelerations -- Treatment / Management
content: After completing a detailed assessment of the etiology of late declaration, immediate intrauterine resuscitative measures are initiated to prevent fetal acidemia and to decrease fetal morbidity and mortality. The resuscitative measures include:

title: Late Decelerations -- Treatment / Management
content: Maternal repositioning to left lateral position, right lateral, or knee-chest position, which relieves the vena cava compression by the gravid uterus - this allows for an increased venous return and cardiac output, which subsequently increases uteroplacental blood flow

title: Late Decelerations -- Treatment / Management
content: Intravenous hydration: Hypotension secondary to epidural anesthesia can also be corrected by giving the mother an intravenous fluid bolus or by alpha-adrenergic agonists administered by the anesthesiologist. Correcting maternal hypotension increases intravascular volume, raises maternal PO 2 , and, eventually, increases uteroplacental blood flow and PO 2 .

title: Late Decelerations -- Treatment / Management
content: Administering supplemental oxygen: There is conflicting data about maternal O 2 administration for Category II and Category III fetal heart tracings. Some observational studies report that O 2 administration can improve fetal oxygenation and decrease decelerations, but overall, the data are conflicting; the standard of practice when a fetal heart tracing abnormality is observed remains to administer supplemental oxygen.

title: Late Decelerations -- Treatment / Management
content: Discontinuing uterotonics: Relaxation of the uterine muscles has been shown to increase uteroplacental blood flow. The frequency of uterine contractions can also be decreased with tocolytics; tocolysis has been shown to improve uterine relaxation by decreasing the frequency of contractions and increasing uteroplacental blood flow.

title: Late Decelerations -- Treatment / Management
content: Expeditious operative vaginal delivery or cesarean delivery: if those mentioned above intrauterine resuscitative measures are not improving the fetal heart tracings and there are persistent late decelerations with loss of variability, then expeditious steps must be taken towards delivering the fetus. [10] [1]

title: Late Decelerations -- Differential Diagnosis
content: The differential diagnoses of late decelerations include: Increasing fetal acidemia Intrauterine umbilical cord compression Maternal/fetal poisoning Nuchal cord entanglements Oligohydramnios Pushing efforts during the second stage of labor Umbilical cord prolapse Uterine fetal acidemia Uterine tachysystole

title: Late Decelerations -- Prognosis
content: The scenario of recurrent late decelerations can be precarious, as they can become hazardous if not promptly evaluated. Evaluating the entire fetal heart tracing and maternal status is essential. Consideration is necessary to the degree of variability and presence, or absence of accelerations, and the underlying cause of the deceleration must be addressed immediately. If the late decelerations are recurrent with minimal or no variability and have not improved with intrauterine resuscitative measures, then expeditious steps must be taken towards delivering the fetus.

title: Late Decelerations -- Complications
content: If recurrent late decelerations with no variability (Category III) persist or are not promptly evaluated and treated, this can lead to increased fetal morbidity and mortality. Complications associated with Category III tracings include fetal acidemia with low APGAR scores, low umbilical cord pH, increased risk of neonatal intensive care unit admission after delivery, neonatal encephalopathy, and cerebral palsy.

title: Late Decelerations -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Labor and delivery management is usually handled by an interprofessional team that includes an obstetrician, a labor and delivery nurse, and a midwife. During some deliveries, one may note recurrent late declarations, which can become hazardous if not promptly evaluated. Evaluating the entire fetal heart tracing and maternal status is critical. The level of variability and presence or absence of accelerations merits strong consideration. Prompt intrauterine resuscitative measures must commence with concurrent correction of the underlying cause of the late deceleration. If the fetal heart tracing is not improved and late decelerations persist, then expeditious steps must be taken towards delivering the fetus. The outcomes for babies treated promptly are excellent. But if there is a delay, the fetus can suffer a severe anoxic injury to the brain. [11]
